passage:
Come here, Neelam, hold this onion. Your Swati Aunty has a story about a like button.

I was twenty. Aman had replied late three nights running, and then I saw him like a photo of a girl from his class. My mind ran wild: she must be his new person, that's why he's busy. I picked up his old diary at his flat and my hand stayed on it.

I put it down. Instead I made two columns on a paper: what I actually saw, and what I imagined. The left column had a late reply and a like. The right column had everything else.

Next day I said, "You've been slow to reply, and it's been worrying me. What's going on?" He'd been helping his brother move house, tired out. I felt small, and lighter.

That paper is still in my cupboard.

qa.q: What had Aman done three nights running?
qa.a: Aman had replied late three nights running.

qa.q: What was Swati thinking when she put the diary down and made two columns?
qa.a: She was trying to separate what she actually saw, a late reply and a like, from what her anxious mind was imagining.

qa.q: What made Swati's question to Aman a better choice than reading his diary?
qa.a: She asked calmly about what was worrying her, so she got the real answer, without spying or accusing him.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt if Swati had read his diary and then confronted him?
qa.a: He might have felt distrusted and invaded, and the real reason for his late replies would have been buried under the quarrel.

grounding: Shows suspicion set off by a late reply and a like, with evidence separated from anxiety and a calm question asked instead of spying.

passage:
Shreya's phone buzzed on the table while she was in the kitchen. Deepak saw the name: Aman. Third time today. His hand actually moved towards the phone. He pulled it back.
When she came out with two bowls of instant noodles, he said, 'Can I ask something without it sounding bad?'
'That's a scary start.'
'I've been feeling suspicious, and I hate it. You've been texting Aman a lot. I nearly looked at your phone just now. I didn't.'
Shreya put the bowls down slowly. 'Thank you for not looking. And for asking.' She unlocked the phone and held it out. He shook his head.
'I don't want to read it. I want to hear it.'
'Aman's organising the surprise for my sister's graduation. I've been hiding it from her, not from you.'
Deepak let out a long breath. 'My brain made a whole movie out of three texts.'
'Next time, ask sooner. Movies are worse than questions.'

qa.q: Who is Aman, according to Shreya?
qa.a: The person organising the surprise for her sister's graduation.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when the phone buzzed?
qa.a: He felt suspicious and anxious, enough that his hand moved towards her phone.

qa.q: What did Deepak do instead of spying?
qa.a: He pulled his hand back and calmly told Shreya his worry, asking to hear the truth rather than read her phone 👍

qa.q: How does Shreya respond to Deepak's question?
qa.a: She thanks him for not looking and for asking, and explains openly.

grounding: Shows a young man whose suspicion rises over a partner's texts, separating anxiety from evidence and asking calmly instead of checking her phone.

passage: Last winter I did something I'm still ashamed of. I'm Lalremsiami, Siami to everyone, and my boyfriend Kishore had started liking every photo a new girl in his office posted. Then his replies got slower. My mind raced: late nights, new friend, likes. One night, while he was in the shower, I unlocked his phone and read his chats. There was nothing. Office jokes, a group chat about a football match, messages to his mum. I sat on the bed feeling sick, not relieved, because I'd just done the very thing I'd hate to have done to me. When he came out, I told him. He was quiet and hurt. 'You could have just asked me.' He was right. What I had was anxiety left over from my last relationship, not evidence. We talked for a long time that night. Now, when the doubt starts, I write down what I actually know, and then I ask him. Calmly. It's worked every time so far.

qa.q: What did Siami find on Kishore's phone?
qa.a: Nothing worrying: office jokes, a football group chat, messages to his mum.

qa.q: How did Siami feel after reading the chats?
qa.a: Siami felt sick and ashamed rather than relieved, having done something that would hurt if done in return.

qa.q: What does Siami do now when doubt starts?
qa.a: Writes down what is actually known, then asks Kishore calmly.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he learned about the phone?
qa.a: Quiet and hurt, wishing Siami had just asked him.

grounding: A first-person account of suspicion leading to secretly checking a partner's phone, then learning to separate anxiety from evidence and ask calmly.
